blocks.content: Ladakh's cold-desert ecology (Chapter 2) supports a distinctive set of high-altitude wildlife species and protected areas found in few other parts of India — a favourite source of species-and-park pairing questions, alongside genuine and pressing contemporary environmental concerns.

cells: Near Leh, extending into the Zanskar range

India's largest national park by area; a major snow leopard habitat, among the best-known snow-leopard-viewing destinations globally; also supports the Tibetan wolf, Ladakh urial and other high-altitude fauna
Protects the high-altitude wetland ecosystems around Tso Moriri and Tso Kar; critical habitat for the black-necked crane, Tibetan wild ass (kiang), and other Trans-Himalayan species
Protects extreme high-altitude habitat, including areas relevant to snow leopard and other rare Trans-Himalayan mammal conservation

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Hemis National Park is frequently cited as India's LARGEST national park by area — a superlative distinct from, and not to be confused with, its equally famous status as a premier snow leopard habitat.

items: Snow leopard — Ladakh (particularly Hemis National Park) is one of the world's best-known locations for snow leopard sightings and research, making the region a globally significant site for high-altitude big-cat conservation and specialised wildlife tourism.

Black-necked crane — a rare, high-altitude crane species found in the Changthang wetlands (Tso Moriri, Tso Kar), holding particular cultural/religious significance in Ladakhi Buddhist tradition alongside its conservation importance.
Tibetan wild ass (kiang) — a large wild equine species found across the Changthang plateau's grasslands, among the most visible large mammals of the region.
Ladakh urial and Himalayan blue sheep (bharal) — key wild ungulate species adapted to Ladakh's high-altitude terrain, also serving as prey species supporting the region's snow leopard population.
Pashmina/Changra goats and yaks, while domesticated rather than wild, remain ecologically and economically central to the Changthang pastoral landscape (Chapter 8).

Glacial retreat across Ladakh's mountain ranges, linked to wider Himalayan climate-change trends, poses a long-term threat to the region's already fragile, glacier-dependent water supply — a concern that directly motivated the 'ice stupa' innovation described in Chapter 8.

Rapid, tourism-driven urban growth in and around Leh has placed significant strain on water supply, waste management, and traditional land-use patterns, prompting growing local and administrative attention to sustainable-tourism planning.

Concerns about unregulated outside investment and land acquisition — heightened following the 2019 removal of Article 35A's protections (Chapter 7) — form a central plank of the environmental dimension of the Sixth Schedule demand, given fears that unregulated development could degrade Ladakh's fragile high-altitude ecosystems.

Ladakh's extreme vulnerability to climate change — as a glacier-and-snowmelt-dependent cold desert with minimal buffering capacity — has made it a prominent case study in Himalayan climate-adaptation discourse, with Sonam Wangchuk's climate-focused activism (Chapter 7) explicitly linking the region's environmental and political demands.
Hemis National Park = India's largest national park by area; premier global snow-leopard habitat.
Changthang Wildlife Sanctuary protects Tso Moriri/Tso Kar wetlands; key habitat for the black-necked crane and Tibetan wild ass (kiang).
Key species: snow leopard, black-necked crane, Tibetan wild ass (kiang), Ladakh urial, Himalayan blue sheep (bharal).
Glacial retreat and tourism-driven urban strain on Leh's water/waste systems are the region's most pressing environmental concerns.
Land-rights/unregulated-investment concerns (post-Article 35A removal) are a core environmental dimension of the Sixth Schedule demand.
